chunks.text: Results Workflow of using ZoomSEM for SEM super-resolution Figure 1: Overview of the ZoomSEM network and speed advantages. a , Workflow of SEM super-resolution using ZoomSEM. Given a low-resolution SEM volume, the ZoomSEM network performs 4 × \times , 8 × \times , or 16 × \times super-resolution without requiring high-resolution acquisition. b , Training pipeline and schematic structure of the ZoomSEM network. c , Estimated improvement in imaging speed when using ZoomSEM. Considering both acquisition and inference time, the overall speedup is 10.0-fold from 16 nm to 4 nm, 21.0-fold from 32 nm to 4 nm, and 29.2-fold from 64 nm to 4 nm. Time estimates are based on a 60 μ \mu m × \times 60 μ \mu m imaging area, corresponding to an image resolution of 15000 × \times 15000 pixels at 4 nm voxel size. The inference time is measured using 8 A100 GPUs. We aim to develop a method that directly predicts high-resolution EM images from low-resolution inputs using a trained network, thereby reducing both imaging cost and acquisition time (Fig. 1 a). This requires both representative training data and an architecture capable of exploiting the 3D spatial structure of serial EM volumes. Existing datasets are limited to small upscaling factors or rely on synthetic degradation that poorly reflects real EM acquisition. We therefore constructed RealSEM-Pair, a 3D serial SEM dataset from mouse entorhinal cortex containing pixel-level aligned volume pairs at four resolutions (4 nm, 16 nm, 32 nm, and 64 nm), registered via a stepwise strategy. Even across a 16-fold resolution gap, our stepwise registration strategy achieves precise pixel-level alignment. Compared to prior datasets, RealSEM-Pair provides up to 16-fold resolution spans from exclusively real acquisitions, with full axial registration and substantially larger scale.

Trained on this dataset, ZoomSEM employs a recurrent transformer architecture with bidirectional propagation across serial sections, and introduces the ADMA module to handle the structural scale variances characteristic of axial adjacent EM sections (Fig. 1 b). As the input resolution decreases, the acceleration gains increase markedly: 16 nm imaging combined with ZoomSEM achieves a 10.0 × \times speedup, 32 nm imaging combined with ZoomSEM achieves a 21.0 × \times speedup, and 64 nm imaging combined with ZoomSEM achieves a 29.2 × \times speedup (Fig. 1 c). These speed improvements account for both acquisition time and model inference time, measured using 8 A100 GPUs to ensure fair and reasonable computational resources. Importantly, imaging speed remains the primary bottleneck in large-scale SEM workflows. A substantial portion of the total imaging time is resolution-independent, including delays from stage movement, coil and field switching, scintillator and photodetector signal conversion, and data buffering or software processing. ZoomSEM excels in SEM super-resolution across various upscaling factors We comprehensively evaluate ZoomSEM on three super-resolution tasks: from 16 nm to 4 nm (4 × \times ), from 32 nm to 4 nm (8 × \times ), and from 64 nm to 4 nm (16 × \times ). Three strong baselines are included for comparison: CFAT (single image super-resolution method) [ 23 ] , IART (video super-resolution method) [ 22 ] , and EMDiffuse (EM super-resolution method) [ 14 ] . We use PSNR, SSIM [ 24 ] , and FSIM [ 25 ] for quantitative assessments. LPIPS [ 26 ] is excluded due to its emphasis on perceptual texture similarity over structural fidelity, which misaligns with the objective of accurately replicating true high-resolution SEM images of cellular structures. The test set comprises four volumes, each containing 177 sections at 1536 × \times 1536 pixels, totalling 708 high-resolution images. As shown in Fig.

2 a, d, and g, ZoomSEM consistently outperforms all baselines in all fidelity metrics. We further assess qualitative outcomes by comparing input and output images (Fig. 2 b, e, and h). For super-resolution from 16 nm to 4 nm (4 × \times ), ZoomSEM closely matches the high-resolution ground truth (GT) and is the only method that accurately reconstructs vesicle locations (Fig. 2 b). For super-resolution from 32 nm to 4 nm (8 × \times ), ZoomSEM maintains high fidelity and resolves fine structures other methods fail to capture (Fig. 2 e). At the extreme 16 × \times magnification (from 64 nm to 4 nm), ZoomSEM recovers most cellular features, despite minor errors, whereas other approaches largely fail (Fig. 2 h). Although EMDiffuse produces outputs stylistically closer to the GT, it introduces numerous incorrect structures. In contrast, ZoomSEM accurately reconstructs cellular ultrastructure, rendering it more suitable for real-world, large-scale EM super-resolution tasks. We also visualize the pixel-wise intensity error in Fig. 2 c, f, i, showing that ZoomSEM consistently produces pixel values closer to the GT than existing methods across all three super-resolution settings. All models are trained under their original training-data pipelines. b,e,h , Qualitative comparison for super-resolution tasks from 16 nm to 4 nm (4 × \times ), from 32 nm to 4 nm (8 × \times ), and from 64 nm to 4 nm (16 × \times ). Arrows in b highlight fine structural details that are restored by our method but not by other methods.

From 16 nm to 4 nm, ZoomSEM closely matches the high-resolution ground truth (GT). From 32 nm to 4 nm, ZoomSEM shows a pronounced advantage, successfully resolving fine structures that other methods fail to reconstruct while maintaining high fidelity. From 64 nm to 4 nm, other methods largely fail to recover meaningful content. Despite minor errors in the internal cellular structures, ZoomSEM recovers the overall cell morphology, even when the input retains almost no discernible details. c,f,i , pixel-wise intensity error comparison along the blue lines in panels b, e, and h. ZoomSEM is compared with baseline methods by measuring the pixel intensity differences along the blue lines, with GT as reference. Advancing SEM super-resolution with real-world training dataset and superior network architecture To validate the necessity of real-world training data, we compared models trained on synthetic degradation pipelines—bicubic downsampling (BD) and the high-order degradation pipeline (HOD) [ 27 ] —against those trained directly on real image pairs. Models trained on synthetic data perform notably worse under real super-resolution scenarios (Fig. 3 a-c), confirming that real paired data are essential for effective EM super-resolution. To demonstrate that the proposed ZoomSEM network itself offers inherent advantages, we trained all baseline methods on the RealSEM-Pair dataset using PSNR, SSIM [ 24 ] , and FSIM [ 25 ] as quantitative metrics, and compared results with CFAT [ 23 ] , IART [ 22 ] , and EMDiffuse [ 14 ] . As illustrated in Fig. 3 d-f, ZoomSEM markedly outperforms these baselines in terms of numerical fidelity. We further perform qualitative comparisons of input and output images (Fig. 3 g-h). For the 32 nm to 4 nm (8 × \times ) task, CFAT+ and IART+ (cf. Fig. 2 e and Fig. 3 g) visibly improve upon CFAT and IART, owing to training on our RealSEM-Pair dataset; nevertheless, ZoomSEM demonstrates superior structural fidelity.

In the more challenging 64 nm to 4 nm (16 × \times ) task, although most methods fail to reconstruct the underlying architecture, ZoomSEM successfully recovers the global cellular morphology (Fig. 3 h). Notably, while IART also employs a recurrent transformer architecture, its alignment module does not fully leverage the spatial correlations in EM images. By contrast, our ADMA module incorporates both affine transformations and sub-pixel-level alignment across EM sections, leading to results that significantly surpass those of IART+. EMDiffuse is already trained on RealSEM-Pair; consequently, no additional dataset refinements are applied in this comparison. At this extreme scale, other methods fail to recover reliable structures, while ZoomSEM reconstructs coherent cellular morphology, yielding segmented results close to the GT. All segmentation was performed fully automatically without manual correction. Accurate downstream segmentation enabled by ZoomSEM To validate the accuracy of ZoomSEM reconstructions in downstream segmentation, we utilized both the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 28 ] , a large deep-learning-based segmentation model, and the conventional Otsu thresholding method [ 29 ] , to automatically segment the EM super-resolution outputs of all methods. Specifically, we employed VOI [ 30 ] to assess SAM-based segmentation results and defined the pixel-level accuracy (ACC) metric to measure consistency with a binarized GT for Otsu-based segmentation. All segmentation procedures were fully automated with no manual refinements. Since the segmentation labels were pseudo-labels generated automatically from the GT, a small degree of error and inconsistencies in mask selection might arise. Nonetheless, the segmentation metrics remained reliable for evaluating overall consistency with the GT. Two key conclusions emerge from these experiments (Fig. 4 ). First, ZoomSEM demonstrates significantly higher semantic consistency with the GT across both SAM- and Otsu-based evaluations compared to other methods. Second, this indicates that ZoomSEM’s outputs more closely align with the GT at the image level. Robust cross-sample and cross-species generalization of ZoomSEM We then investigate the cross-sample and cross-species generalization capabilities of ZoomSEM. To evaluate cross-sample generalization under large-scale dataset, we used a 32 nm low-resolution SEM dataset acquired from the mouse striatum.

We selected a central region of interest with a field of view of 5120 × \times 5120 pixels at 32 nm resolution and acquired 900 serial sections. Two sections with poor imaging quality were excluded. After axial registration, patch extraction, and brightness normalization, inference was performed on the remaining 898 slices using a ZoomSEM network trained on the RealSEM-Pair dataset (from mouse entorhinal cortex), without any fine-tuning. The resulting super-resolved volume totaled approximately 795GB. As shown in Fig. 5 a, ZoomSEM significantly enhances the resolution of the low-resolution input volume. It reveals clear cell boundaries and intracellular organelle structures that are not visible in the original input. Moreover, Otsu-based binarization highlights structural features that are absent in the low-resolution data but successfully reconstructed by ZoomSEM (Fig. 5 b). Figure 6: ZoomSEM facilitates ultrastructure recovery. a , Synapses under three EM super-resolution settings: from 16 nm to 4 nm, from 32 nm to 4 nm, and from 64 nm to 4 nm. Comparing ZoomSEM to input, synaptic clefts transform from blurred or imperceptible to clearly defined and detailed from 16 nm to 4 nm, become distinguishable again from 32 nm to 4 nm (after being virtually lost), and emerge from near-complete absence at from 64 nm to 4 nm to reveal a recognizable synaptic outline. b , Synaptic vesicles at the same three EM super-resolution scales. ZoomSEM faithfully reconstructs vesicles (yellow arrows) when super-resolving from 16 nm and 32 nm to 4 nm. Although vesicles are unresolved in the 64 nm to 4 nm setting, the synaptic cleft is still clearly visible (between red arrows), so the synapse remains easy to recognize. c , Spine neck at three EM super-resolution scales. The ultra-thin neck of the dendritic spine is successfully recovered in all three super-resolution settings. d , Mitochondria at three EM super-resolution scales. ZoomSEM faithfully recovers mitochondrial cristae from 32 nm to 4 nm super-resolution.

e , Microvilli at three EM super-resolution scales using ZoomSEM-FT. Larger microvilli indicated by red arrows are accurately reconstructed across all scales, while finer microvillar structures (green arrows) are faithfully recovered from 16 nm to 4 nm and from 32 nm to 4 nm, but remain unresolved in the 64 nm to 4 nm setting. f , Manual tracing on the 32 nm to 4 nm super-resolved volume reconstructs an axon bouton-dendritic spine pair, and short segments of the axon terminal and dendrite are further traced. Left, a representative section with hand-drawn annotations. Right, the resulting 3D tracing. We also validated the cross-species generalization capability of ZoomSEM, expanding its utility from connectome mapping to broader life science applications. We constructed a small-scale human breast cell acini dataset. The acini samples were derived from Jorgens et al. [ 31 ] , and we re-imaged them under the same pipeline described above. This dataset comprises 200 serial EM sections with pixel-level alignment across multiple resolutions. We used the first 100 sections to fine-tune ZoomSEM, reserving the remaining 100 for testing; the fine-tuned network is referred to as ZoomSEM-FT. We then compared ZoomSEM-FT with ZoomSEM, CFAT, and IART, each trained from scratch on 100 acini images, by evaluating their performance on the validation set from two perspectives: visual quality and consistency with the GT segmentation. On the acini dataset, ZoomSEM already outperforms the two baseline methods in quantitative metrics. Moreover, ZoomSEM-FT significantly surpasses ZoomSEM, especially in SSIM and VOI (Fig. 5 c-d), suggesting that the fine-tuned network achieves substantially better structural similarity. Qualitative comparisons further corroborate these findings (Fig. 5 e-f).

Notably, at 64 nm to 4 nm (16 × \times ) upscaling, other methods (including ZoomSEM) fail to reconstruct the more homogeneous texture of acini, whereas ZoomSEM-FT—benefiting from the data priors obtained from the RealSEM-Pair dataset—achieves marked improvements in fidelity and segmentation consistency with the GT. These results highlight two key outcomes. First, ZoomSEM consistently outperforms all baselines, confirming that its performance advantages on the mouse entorhinal cortex data generalize to the acini dataset. Second, the fine-tuned variant ZoomSEM-FT further improves reconstruction quality, demonstrating the value of RealSEM-Pair as an effective training prior. In effect, ZoomSEM trained on the RealSEM-Pair dataset serves as a transferable foundation model, capable of generalizing to new imaging contexts. Notably, it achieves strong performance in cross-sample settings without any additional training data, and can be adapted to cross-species datasets with only a modest amount of registered image pairs (just 100 in this case). Ultrastructure recovery with ZoomSEM We assess the practical implications of ZoomSEM by analyzing its output image quality on key subcellular structures (including synapses, synaptic vesicles, spine necks, mitochondria and microvilli), its impact on downstream 3D neuron reconstruction accuracy, and the acceleration of imaging throughput achieved by leveraging ZoomSEM. Applying super-resolution techniques to visualize synaptic structures with greater clarity is crucial for uncovering the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal communication, synaptic plasticity, and pathology [ 32 , 33 ] . Across 16 nm to 4 nm, 32 nm to 4 nm, and 64 nm to 4 nm super-resolution tasks, ZoomSEM enhances synaptic clefts from being blurred or imperceptible to clearly distinguishable structures, with fine details at 16 nm, recoverable synapses at 32 nm, and even recognizable cellular contours at 64 nm (Fig. 6 a).

Applying super-resolution to accurately visualize synaptic vesicles is paramount for elucidating the molecular mechanisms of neurotransmitter release, vesicle recycling, and activity-dependent membrane trafficking at synapses [ 34 , 35 ] . With ZoomSEM super-resolution, synaptic vesicles can be visualized distinctly and correctly (Fig. 6 b), enabling direct inspection of vesicle pools within a single axon bouton. Dendritic spines—key postsynaptic sites for excitatory signaling—also benefit markedly from ZoomSEM. Resolving their morphology is essential for understanding synaptic plasticity and biochemical compartmentalization [ 36 ] . Notably, the ultra-thin spine neck, which is usually the most difficult substructure to discern, is faithfully recovered under all three super-resolution settings (Fig. 6 c). Mitochondria are another key structure; their cristae organize the oxidative-phosphorylation machinery to sustain adenosine triphosphate production [ 37 , 38 ] , and ZoomSEM faithfully recovers cristae from 32 nm to 4 nm super-resolution (Fig. 6 d). Applying super-resolution to precisely visualize microvillar architecture is essential for elucidating their roles in epithelial absorption and mucosal defence, as microvilli are actin-supported apical-membrane protrusions that assemble into an ordered brush border, thereby expanding surface area and enriching transporters and enzymes [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] . ZoomSEM-FT restores microvillar structures that are indiscernible at low-resolution imaging (Fig. 6 e). Specifically, densely packed microvillar regions remain unresolvable at 32 nm imaging but are successfully reconstructed by ZoomSEM-FT (green arrow, Fig. 6 e). Larger microvillar structures ( ∼ \sim 200 nm diameter) are indistinguishable at 64 nm imaging but are accurately reconstructed by ZoomSEM-FT (red arrow, Fig. 6 e). Finally, we selected the 32 nm to 4 nm super-resolution model as a compromise between imaging throughput and reconstruction fidelity.

Using this model, we manually traced and reconstructed an axon bouton-dendritic spine pair, including short segments of the axon terminal and dendrite. As shown in Fig. 6 f, even the thinnest spine neck is faithfully recovered, demonstrating the feasibility of our approach for practical imaging applications. In summary, ZoomSEM significantly accelerates imaging while maintaining high reliability, demonstrating its potential to transform EM imaging workflows, enhance biological research efficiency, and drive scientific discovery. Discussion Serial electron microscopy serves as the cornerstone for mapping large-scale neural circuits at nanometer resolution but is hindered by severe throughput limitations. Standard single-beam scanning electron microscopes require months or even years to image brain volumes at scales of hundreds of micrometers. Advanced multi-beam SEM systems can image substantially faster but remain largely inaccessible due to high financial barriers. This limitation significantly constrains large-scale connectomic studies, making high-resolution serial EM challenging to use for many research groups. In this paper, we introduce ZoomSEM, a deep learning-based method that restores high-resolution SEM images from rapidly acquired low-resolution scans, enabling substantial acceleration without sacrificing structural fidelity. Unlike conventional super-resolution methods trained on synthetic datasets, ZoomSEM leverages a unique, real-world dataset, RealSEM-Pair, comprising precisely registered low- and high-resolution EM image pairs. The use of real-world paired data is critical, as low-resolution EM images capture authentic degradation characteristics, including noise, aberrations, and staining variations, which cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic data. By combining real-world training data with an advanced transformer-based architecture, ZoomSEM effectively reconstructs ultrastructural features from initial resolutions up to 16 × 16\times coarser, translating into data acquisition speedup of approximately 10 to nearly 30 times.

This dramatically improves the utility of standard single-beam SEMs, enabling their imaging performance to approach costly multi-beam instruments and democratizing access to high-throughput volumetric EM. To our knowledge, this is the first approach tailored for large-factor EM super-resolution in real-world settings. ZoomSEM reliably preserves fine biological details, including synapses, synaptic vesicles, spine necks, mitochondria, microvilli, and organelle morphologies across different species and tissue types, demonstrating robust cross-domain generalization, underscoring its potential as a broadly applicable tool in neurobiology and cell biology. Our RealSEM-Pair dataset itself represents a valuable resource for the EM community, enabling rigorous benchmarking and training of future computational methods on authentic imaging data. The accelerated imaging provided by ZoomSEM substantially impacts downstream analyses, notably automated segmentation and connectome reconstruction. By producing high-fidelity reconstructions from low-resolution input, ZoomSEM consistently achieves higher consistency with ground truth (GT) segmentation than baseline methods, particularly at larger upscaling factors. Even in challenging cases where other approaches fail to recover recognizable cellular structures, ZoomSEM preserves key ultrastructural features with sufficient accuracy to support reliable instance interpretation. This advancement enables researchers to undertake comprehensive brain-wide mapping or investigate ultrastructural pathology at scales previously impractical with existing SEM hardware. Despite its strengths, ZoomSEM has boundaries that merit consideration. The method is currently demonstrated on SEM data. Extending it to other EM modalities might require additional training data and potential architectural adjustments. Image artifacts, such as section defects, charging, or contamination, etc., are not explicitly handled.

Moreover, although a model trained on mouse entorhinal cortex generalizes reasonably well to mouse striatum, its performance remains inferior to a counterpart fine-tuned directly on striatal data—reflecting domain gaps introduced by sample preparation, imaging hardware, and brain-region-specific contrast. To deploy ZoomSEM on other specimens or microscopes, one can follow our training pipeline to acquire a modest number of paired images and fine-tune the released model, thereby improving accuracy on the target domain. Generalizing to extremely low signal conditions (e.g. ultra-fast scans with very low dose) may also demand further model robustness. Future efforts will extend ZoomSEM’s capabilities to more diverse EM modalities, imaging conditions and sample types. Incorporating artifact detection or robust loss functions could further improve reliability. Additionally, exploring unsupervised or semi-supervised learning approaches may help reduce dependence on paired ground truth data. Finally, integrating ZoomSEM with downstream segmentation tools into fully automated pipelines could ultimately establish end-to-end workflows for rapid, accurate and scalable connectomic and cellular imaging studies. In summary, ZoomSEM significantly redefines the speed and scale at which volumetric EM imaging can be conducted. By bridging the gap between high-resolution quality and rapid imaging, ZoomSEM stands to transform the accessibility and feasibility of ambitious connectomics and ultrastructural biology studies.
